text: I think we talk too much about trees in cities as if they're just decorative, nice to have but not need to have. That's becoming very outdated. The climate is changing, air quality is getting worse. People have terrible mental health. We need trees in our cities because they are actually some of the most cost-effective ways for us to create healthier, more resilient, more equitable cities. So I think it should be a priority that every city has more trees. Not as an option, as a priority. In terms of climate and environment, the benefits are already huge. They reduce the urban heat island effect. So areas in the city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding areas. And trees help to shade and reduce the temperature. Canopy has shown to reduce the temperature of a street by several degrees. That can actually reduce deaths, reduce heat-related illness. Trees clean our air. They absorb CO2, they produce oxygen, they capture particulate matter. They capture stormwater. So they actually reduce flooding and reduce pressure on our aging stormwater systems. That's extremely important in climate change. Beyond climate, trees are incredibly good for mental health. There's a huge body of literature that says just the fact that we have access to green space, we feel less stress, we concentrate better, we have better mental health. For kids, they play, they learn, they explore. It's very healthy. Adults, if they walk under trees, their blood pressure goes down, they recover attention. Hospitals that have trees view recover faster. They need less painkillers. Trees are also incredibly good for community and local economies. They tend to increase property values. They increase foot traffic. Less crime. It's very healthy for commerce. It makes our streets more walkable. It makes us less car dependent. If we plant in lower income neighborhoods, which have less trees and more heat and more pollution, it's very important for equity. For environmental justice. So yes, trees are important. The only concern is that they require maintenance. They require water. Young trees die very easily if not properly maintained. We need to plant the right species in the right place. Otherwise, they can crack the sidewalks, they can block your views, they can increase allergies. We have to plan well. We have to diversify species. We have to engage the community. We have to budget for maintenance. Trees can sometimes be a pressure factor for gentrification, for green gentrification. People are afraid that if I plant trees, my property value will increase, my rents will increase, and I'll be displaced. And that can happen. Trees can hit power lines, they can hit infrastructure, pipes and so on. But I think it's a very healthy ecosystem. I think that if we plant them properly, if we take care of them, the benefits far outweigh the disadvantages. Cities without trees are very expensive. Much more expensive than the cost of maintenance. So they are like the skeleton of the city. They are the backbone. They clean our air, they cool our streets, they calm our minds, they connect our neighborhoods. They connect people. If we take care of them, if we invest in them, we will have a more healthy and resilient and equitable city. And we should do that.
